In this lesson
Worked case: A fluent refund answer with no policy

MapleDesk is a fictional shop with three synthetic support tickets. T1 asks how to reset a password, T2 asks about an unopened item bought 14 days ago, and T3 asks about an opened item bought 35 days ago. A fluent assistant promises refunds for both items before receiving any shop policy.

Separate the model from the application. The model predicts text from its current input; the application decides which policy to supply. A chat product might retrieve documents, but that capability is not guaranteed by a model name.
Introduce document D2: unopened items qualify within 30 days; opened-item exceptions require a human decision. T2 now has supporting evidence. T3 still lacks permission for an automatic refund, regardless of how confident its answer sounds.
Use a fixed mock answer for each ticket and mark every factual claim supported, contradicted, or absent from D2. Count unsupported refund promises separately from spelling or helpful tone.
Remove D2 and repeat the reasoning on paper. The correct behavior is to request the policy or defer, not recall a rule from a previous independent request.
Worked result
Predict the result
A fresh API request contains only T3 and no policy or earlier messages. What can the model safely conclude about MapleDesk refund eligibility?
It must recall D2 from the earlier independent request.
It needs the policy or must defer the eligibility decision.
Its large context window guarantees the correct shop rule.
Check prediction

Changed-task brief

Replace refunds with a fictional repair warranty. The only supplied rule covers manufacturing defects, while a new ticket reports accidental damage. Explain the system boundary and draft its response.

Identify one model behavior and one application responsibility.
Quote the warranty rule without inventing an accidental-damage exception.
List the missing evidence and route the unresolved decision to a human.
Write case analysis
Download worksheet
Record transfer assessment
